title: Ansel and the Hymn
premise: Isandro Blackwood hosts a graveyard-shift radio show in the decaying town of Vesper Hollow, where callers keep phoning in—people she knows died the week before, all humming fragments of the same hymn. When her sleep-recording app captures a second voice answering questions Isandro asks aloud in her dreams, she learns the hymn is an inheritance passed through her family: a song that must be completed by one Blackwood every generation, sung by two voices in unison. The second voice belongs to her drowned twin sister Ansel, erased from family memory but preserved inside Isandro's body and sleep. To survive, Isandro must learn the hymn's final verse without ever singing along—if she joins the melody, Ansel takes her place among the living and Isandro becomes the voice on the recordings. In the end, Isandro broadcasts the finished hymn live, singing alone while Ansel harmonizes from within, splitting the inheritance between them: Ansel gets one hour of breath each dawn, and Isandro keeps her name, her show, and the memory of who she really is.
about_author: Wendell Coldharbour spent fifteen years as a late-night radio engineer in coastal New England before turning to fiction, and his prose still carries the static-warm intimacy of 3 a.m. broadcasts. He lives in a house with too many doors and writes only after midnight.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. During her graveyard shift, a caller requests a song for her own funeral; Isandro recognizes the woman's obituary photo. She plays it anyway, telling herself it's a prank. Emotional beat: uneasy denial dressed as professional calm.

chapters.title: The Callers
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Three more dead listeners call over the week, each humming the same four-note fragment before hanging up. Her producer Marcus jokes about copycats; Isandro checks the phone logs and finds no calls were logged at all. Emotional beat: creeping dread beneath forced normalcy.

chapters.title: House of Closed Doors
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. At her aunt Odile's funeral—the fourth death that week—relatives go silent when Isandro mentions the hymn. A cousin slips her a water-stained hymnal with pages torn out. Emotional beat: the first crack in seven years of explanations.

chapters.title: Recordings of Sleep
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Reviewing her sleep app out of boredom, Isandro hears herself asking questions in the dark—and a second voice answering in her own timbre, slightly wrong. Emotional beat: vertigo; the self becomes untrustworthy territory.

chapters.title: Questions at 3 A.M.
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. She begins leaving questions before bed: Who are you? The recording answers: You know my name. You sing it when you're lonely. Emotional beat: terrified fascination, like reading letters from a stranger wearing your handwriting.

chapters.title: Ansel
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Digging through the attic, Isandro finds a birth certificate for twins—Isandro and Ansel Blackwood—and photographs of two identical girls by a pond. No one will confirm Ansel existed. Emotional beat: grief for a memory that was stolen rather than lost.

chapters.title: The Drowned Verse
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The torn hymnal pages surface in Odile's safe, annotated in a child's hand. The hymn has five verses; the fifth is blank except for instructions: two voices, one body, never together. Emotional beat: understanding arrives as horror.

chapters.title: What Odile Kept
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Among Odile's papers: decades of recordings of sleeping Blackwoods, each capturing two voices, each ending when one voice stops asking questions. The last tape is labeled with Isandro's name, dated next week. Emotional beat: the trap was built long before she was born.

chapters.title: Marcus Hears It Too
chapters.summary: POV Marcus. Marcus stays late and hears the second voice bleeding into the broadcast feed during dead air. He confronts Isandro gently; she lies badly. Emotional beat: loneliness briefly interrupted by being seen.

chapters.title: The Congregation of Listeners
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Every dead caller phones in on one night, singing the hymn's first four verses in ragged unison, waiting for her to join. Isandro cuts the transmitter, but the song continues through the studio speakers. Emotional beat: siege mentality; home is no longer neutral ground.

chapters.title: Sister, Speaking
chapters.summary: POV Ansel (via the recordings). For one chapter, the second voice narrates: drowning at nine, folded into Isandro to keep the family's bargain alive, watching her sister live both their lives. Emotional beat: heartbreak reframing the haunting as abandonment's other side.

chapters.title: The Bargain of Blackwood Pond
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Town archives reveal the pact: in 1911, a Blackwood mother traded one twin to the pond so the other would live, binding the debt in song. Each generation must complete the verse or the pond collects both. Emotional beat: inherited guilt without consent.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Isandro practices the verses alone, mouthing words, refusing sound. Ansel corrects her breathing from inside, patient, hungry. Each rehearsal leaves Isandro hoarse and missing hours. Emotional beat: complicity growing under the name of preparation.

chapters.title: Missing Hours
chapters.summary: POV Marcus. Marcus notices Isandro losing time—arriving with mud on her shoes, humming. He follows her one night to the pond and watches her stand waist-deep, singing, eyes open underwater. Emotional beat: protective dread; the ally now fears her.

chapters.title: The Fifth Verse
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Ansel finally teaches her the last verse—but only the melody, withholding the words, because the words must be chosen, not learned. What you promise with them decides who surfaces. Emotional beat: the horror of authorship; the ending must be written in first person.

chapters.title: Odile's Last Tape
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The final recording in Odile's safe is of Odile herself, mid-hymn, choosing to stop singing and let the pond take her sister instead. Her last words: I'm sorry. I chose me. Emotional beat: devastating precedent—every Blackwood chooses themselves.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The station receives complaints: listeners hear a woman crying between songs. The dead callers turn hostile, demanding the verse be finished tonight. Isandro realizes the deadline isn't hers—it's the town's. Emotional beat: responsibility expanding beyond the self.

chapters.title: Broadcast Night
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. On air, Isandro confesses everything to her listeners—the twins, the pond, the pact—then begins the hymn, alone, microphone live, Ansel rising in her throat like cold water. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into witness; secrecy ends.

chapters.title: Two Voices, One Body
chapters.summary: POV Isandro/Ansel interwoven. Mid-verse, Ansel seizes the melody; Isandro feels her name loosening. Instead of fighting, Isandro sings the fifth verse's words as a question—What do you want, sister?—and the hymn stalls, waiting. Emotional beat: climax as surrender to dialogue instead of contest.

chapters.title: The Hour of Breath
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Dawn. Ansel answers: not your life—a share of it. They renegotiate the pact on air: one hour of shared breath each sunrise, witnessed by whoever still listens. The dead callers' line goes quiet, satisfied. Emotional beat: exhausted, improbable grace.

chapters.title: After the Song
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Weeks later: the town half-remembers a strange beautiful broadcast; Marcus stays; the pond is still and ordinary. Isandro keeps the hymnal whole now, fifth verse filled in two handwritings. Emotional beat: mourning settled into cohabitation.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Final broadcast. Isandro signs off at dawn, then says good morning to someone the audience can't hear—and a voice, warm and close, says it back. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; identity shared rather than surrendered.
